Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Writing and Language — "the writing style's ability to engage and captivate readers"
- **thin_for_its_length** (warning only) — the scene is near its word target and carries one beat's worth of content, padded with restatement, weather, or interiority that repeats itself. The grader penalises this and the length score does not reward it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **costless_conflict** (warning only) — a conflict resolved without costing anybody anything specific. Partial and temporary resolutions are fine; free ones read as unearned.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Emotional Impact — "the story's ability to evoke strong and deep emotional impact"
- **theme_stated** (warning only) — a sentence that explains what the story means, rather than a choice that tests it. Quote the sentence — it is almost always removable without loss.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Themes — "how well the themes are explored throughout the story"
- **flat_diction** (warning only) — constructions repeating within the scene, filter verbs standing in for perception ("she felt that", "he realised that"), abstraction where a concrete detail belongs, or sentence rhythm that does not move with the tension.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Writing and Language; LongBench-Write Clarity — "confusing expression with minimal details"
- **inert_open_or_close** (warning only) — the scene opens on setting or mood rather than a situation already in motion, or closes on a mood rather than a specific next beat — an unanswered question, a door about to open. In a long story this is what decides whether the reader turns over.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Reading Experience; LongStoryEval Enjoyment and Engagement
- **genre_promise_unmet** (warning only) — the scene declines the obligation its genre carries — a horror scene with nothing at stake, a romance scene with no charge between the two people, a mystery scene that advances no inference. Breaking a genre promise deliberately is legitimate; it has to be visibly deliberate.
    penalised by: LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment; LongBench-Write Relevance

Two rules, both enforced by the tool rather than left to your judgement:

Only these may be **error** and therefore cost the writer a round: off_brief, restates_prior_scene, nothing_changes, internal_incoherence, ending_not_delivered.
Everything else is a warning — it reaches the writer and costs nothing. That asymmetry is
deliberate: a craft judgement a reader could reasonably disagree with must not be able to
hold up a scene.

And a blocking craft finding needs **checkable evidence**, in the shape the check names.
Either two verbatim quotes (this draft, and the earlier passage it repeats or the half of
itself it contradicts), or a named state pair — what is true when the scene opens and what
is true when it closes. `nothing_changes` is precisely the claim that you cannot name a
difference, so name both halves and let the pair be the evidence. If you cannot produce
the evidence, you have an impression: report it as a warning, which is a perfectly useful
thing to do.

`suggestion` is mandatory on every craft finding, warnings included. The writer cannot see
the manuscript, the index or the rubric. A craft note without an instruction is a complaint
it can only answer by guessing, and a guessed craft repair damages prose that was working —
which is not hypothetical: a run whose findings the writer could not act on scored 8.4
points below one with fewer, better ones.

At most two craft findings can block one round, whatever you report. Consistency comes
first when both are present: it is counted by name and craft is not. So if you have three
craft blockers, the third is a warning — pick the two that most damage the scene.

## What the orchestrator asked for on this scene

Check the draft against continuity and craft rules: verify period accuracy for Windsor 1956 (no anachronistic language, correct press mechanics), ensure staff roles and private routines are plausible, and flag any unsupported claims. Also judge craft: pacing, scene shape, and whether the Queen's interiority remains appropriately restrained. List each finding with precise provenance.

That is in addition to your standing instructions above, not instead of them.
If it states a story fact that is not in your packet — a name, a measurement, a
quotation, a piece of history — that fact has not been checked against the index by
anyone. Ask about it or establish it yourself in the state delta. Do not write it down
as though it were already true.

## P0

### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Introduce Windsor in summer 1956 through sensory detail and establish the Queen's daily routines and inner restraint.
Present: char-queen, loc-windsor-castle, loc-long-walk, char-lady, char-butler, loc-royal-kitchen, loc-queen-apartment
Target length: about 1212 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

In the summer of 1956 at Windsor, a reigning Queen and a Hollywood actress meet privately before protocol can put them on a stage; a single unscheduled encounter forces both to confront what they must hide and what they might risk, with consequences that quietly reshape reputation, loyalty, and the private habits that sustain public life.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-queen: The reigning monarch, early thirties in 1956: composed, duty-bound, private beneath the ceremonial surface.
- char-actress: A Hollywood film starlet in her late twenties, glamorous, worldly, accustomed to public performance but hungry for private truth.
- char-lady: A senior lady-in-waiting: loyal, fluent in palace protocol, the guardian of household intimacy and unwritten rules.
- char-press: The Queen's press liaison: pragmatic, risk-averse, expert at containing stories and managing the monarch's public image.
- char-confidante: The actress's confidante and manager: protective, commercially minded, experienced with studios and tabloid hunger.
- char-neighbor: A local Windsor neighbor: middle-class, rooted in the town's rhythms, observant of comings and goings and a foil to high drama.
- char-butler: The senior royal butler: meticulous about meals, timings and the small domestic choreographies that keep dignity intact.
- char-gardener: Head gardener at Windsor: earthy, taciturn, keeper of the castle's green rooms and witness to private promenades.
- char-driver: A driver for the actress's party: discreet, practical, used to ferrying fame between studios and salons.
- char-assistant: A junior aide in the royal household: eager, impressionable, helpful and often the bridge between senior staff and minor errands.
- loc-windsor-castle: The castle as locus: state rooms and private apartments, ramparts and terraces, bureaucratic intimacy and centuries of habit.
- loc-long-walk: The Long Walk and Great Park: avenues and summer light, public vistas that still permit private movement at their edges.
- loc-queen-apartment: The Queen's private apartments within the castle: a small, carefully curated domestic world behind official facades.
- loc-guest-cottage: A comfortable, discreet country cottage near Windsor where the actress and her entourage are staying.
- loc-riverside-terrace: A low stone terrace along the Thames near Windsor: secluded, cooled by river breezes, chosen for privacy.
- loc-stable-yard: The castle's stable yard and service passages: where servants move and where public polish meets private industry.
- loc-town-high-street: Windsor's high street: tea rooms, a cinema, small shops and an atmosphere of summer tourism and local gossip.
- loc-railway-station: Windsor & Eton station: arrival point for visitors, belching steam, porters and telegram dispatches.
- loc-royal-kitchen: The vast, warm royal kitchen: cooks, orders, and the social choreography of meals as statecraft and comfort.
- loc-garden-pavilion: A small garden pavilion on castle grounds: discreet for conversation, shaded and intimate.
- loc-teashop: A modest tea shop on the high street where townspeople gather and where ordinary perceptions of the royals and visitors meet.
- obj-invitation-card: A pale, embossed card intended for an official, ceremonial introduction between households.
- obj-silk-handkerchief: A small silk handkerchief—an object exchanged in the private meeting and later kept as memory.
- obj-polaroid-photo: A single, unstable photographic print taken privately, a potential proof of the encounter.
- obj-press-telegrams: Stacks of arrival notices and press queries: the mechanical, nervous apparatus of mid-century news flow.
- obj-journal: The Queen's private journal: ruled pages for small truths, personal reflections that are never published.
- obj-script: A film script the actress carries: a symbol of her work-life and a literal object she reads to pass time.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: third person omniscient, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- The story is set in the summer of 1956 in Windsor; period technology and social institutions (no mobile phones, no internet, reliance on telegrams, print press, radio) must be respected.
- The novel must avoid inventing major public actions or official events for the Queen that contradict established historical fact for 1956; invented private interactions and small domestic details are allowed.
- The private meeting between the Queen and the actress is fictional but must be plausible within 1956 protocol and social norms; no implausible modern behaviours or anachronistic speech.
- Any claim about press coverage, photographs, or public reaction must be plausible for the pre-digital, 1950s British and international press environment.
- Objects and entities listed in the plan are the canonical identifiers; later scenes and state records must only refer to those ids and no new primary characters, locations or significant objects may be introduced without updating the plan.
- The narrative voice is third person omniscient and will occasionally enter interiority but will not claim access to unverifiable private thoughts beyond what characters plausibly guard.
- Secrecy is to be treated seriously: no scene may present a public, verifiable record of the private meeting; any physical proof (photograph, object) must be ambiguous, contested, or carefully controlled within the story.

### writer-guidance-1956-walks  <HARNESS.md>

Guidance: When staging a private walk in 1956 Windsor, the writer may choose between two plausible approaches (recorded as choices rather than facts):

1) Formal discretion: A lady-in-waiting accompanies the sovereign on foot; a small number of household staff (a footman or butler) remain in a visible-but-distant position, timed to intercept if needed. No motor transport accompanies the walk unless by prior notice. This fits a cautious, protocol-minded Queen.

2) Intimate privacy: The Queen slips away escorted only by a trusted lady-in-waiting; household staff are informed later to maintain secrecy, with the butler responsible for timing meals and ensuring the Queen's absence does not disrupt state calls. This fits a Queen who values privacy and trusts inner staff.

The index lacks a definitive protocol; the writer should pick one and write its choice into the state delta to avoid inventing unrecorded facts silently.

## The draft

The Queen began the morning in the small domestic orbit she had kept for herself at Windsor: a single room of pale curtains, a brass kettle, a row of shoes lined as if for inspection. She did not open the heavy doors that looked over the park until the servants had finished their first round; habit held the day together. She made tea with the same motion each time—the tea bag pinched and counted by the same invisible metronome—and sat with her hands warmed by the cup while the house set about its more public rhythms.

The butler arrived with the day's ledger and a quietled face. He moved as he always did through the apartment: a practised economy of gait, a carriage of small ceremonies. He laid the ledger on the table and, without being asked, set out the note of luncheon possibilities in his careful hand. The kettle hissed and the Queen watched the thin steam as though it were a thing that answered her questions.

"One thing," she said, when the ledger had been read and the butler's voice had returned to its neutral cadence. "I should like a walk. The Long Walk, if you please."

The butler inclined his head with the simple fidelity of his kind. "Very good, Ma'am. Shall I tell the kitchen to prepare a basket?"

She shook her head. "No basket. Keep the house to hand. A small cold tray will do if I'm back by lunch."

He made a small note. "We will make provisions. I will keep the household flexible. The kitchen will put together something—sliced cold chicken, open sandwiches and fruit—should you return hungry. I will also inform the senior staff of your absence."

He spoke as if from duty; she heard his duty as a shield rather than an instruction. The choice he offered—flexibility rather than fanfare—fit the small private world she wanted to hold. It was not a refusal of the world's rules so much as a shrinking of ceremony until it could be carried at arm's length.

The lady-in-waiting arrived shortly, efficient and luminous in the way of those who practiced stillness. She stood at the door and folded her hands in the old way; there was a steadiness to her expression that the Queen had learned to lean on. When the Queen said, plainly, "I would like a walk," the lady's fingers tightened for the briefest instant and then relaxed into her answer.

"Of course, Ma'am. When shall we go?"

They walked out together with no fanfare. There was no footman in livery at the gate; there was no motorcar waiting to hum them somewhere else. The butler had been informed, the kitchen had been told to keep a small tray ready, and the household would fold the moment into the day. The Queen liked it that way: the world politely unmade so she could be small and otherwise.

The Long Walk lay precisely as it always did in summer—an avenue of light and green that seemed at once public and private. People took photographs from its edges and picnicked at its shoulder; yet there were places along it where two women could walk without feeling watched. They kept to one of those places: the avenue near the garden pavilion, where a line of elms made a ceiling and the gravel kept their steps honest.

A gardener was there at the pavilion, sleeves rolled and straw hat low, attending to the beds of tea-roses. He lifted a hand by way of greeting; his presence was a piece of the castle's machinery, as much a part of the place as the stones. He did not come close enough to overhear. The Queen appreciated that distance the way one appreciated the margin between stage and wings.

They walked with the particular rhythm of two people who had practiced not to disturb the other: silence tightened into a comfortable pattern and then opened. The Queen said small things at first—about the light, about the way the elms kept the sun from sinking into the park. The lady-in-waiting answered in the neutral, luminous way that had carried her through state dinners and private confidences.

There was a moment—no more than a pause—when the Queen let the thought that usually lived folded in her notebook press at the corner of a sentence. "It is odd," she said, looking straight ahead, "how public everything feels even when one is alone."

The lady-in-waiting did not attempt to soften the statement. She only matched it with a small truth of her own: "One learns to be watched for the sake of it. One also learns to keep the rest of oneself out of sight, because it is safer."

They spoke of loneliness then, not as a complaint but as the fact beneath the trappings. The Queen's voice did not rise; it collected and set down. She spoke of evenings when the lights went out and the house seemed larger than it should, of days that were supposed to be full of meaning but which felt, in private, like a series of obligations. The lady-in-waiting listened as a person who kept confidences for a living, with the kind of attention that was not a question.

"You do what is required of you," the lady said finally. "But you do not have to carry it as though there were only one shoulder convenient for it. There are hands that will hold it if you ask."

The Queen smiled in the way she sometimes did when a practical sentence landed where sentiment could not reach. "I am grateful for that. It is not a thing to say aloud often."

They turned back the way they had come. The gravel kept its small music. The gardener bent again to his roses and the long light made a last soft pass between the trunks. When the Queen reached the apartments again she paused in the doorway, taking in the sight of the kettle on the hob and the ledger folded as if nothing had happened.

The butler was waiting inside, not at her elbow but present; he offered his usual report of messages and dressing plans and then allowed a small, private courtesy as she closed the door behind her.

"Everything in the house was kept to allow your absence, Ma'am," he said. "The kitchen prepared a cold tray, as requested."

She let out a breath that might once have been called a laugh. "Very good. Bring it to the table. I will write for a moment—only a note."

She opened the journal, though she did not write long. The day had already changed shape: the walk had cost her nothing public but it had also given her, quietly, an altered view of the day to come. Outside, the park moved with its usual small dramas; inside, the household resumed its choreography. A private thing had been done in a public place and the world had not noticed.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds

**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the

**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt

**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior

**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an

prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

The Queen began the morning in the small domestic orbit she had kept for herself at Windsor: a single room of pale curtains, a brass kettle, a row of shoes lined as if for inspection. She did not open the heavy doors that looked over the park until the servants had finished their first round; habit held the day together. She made tea with the same motion each time—the tea bag pinched and counted by the same invisible metronome—and sat with her hands warmed by the cup while the house set about its more public rhythms.

The butler arrived with the day's ledger and a quietled face. He moved as he always did through the apartment: a practised economy of gait, a carriage of small ceremonies. He laid the ledger on the table and, without being asked, set out the note of luncheon possibilities in his careful hand. The kettle hissed and the Queen watched the thin steam as though it were a thing that answered her questions.

"One thing," she said, when the ledger had been read and the butler's voice had returned to its neutral cadence. "I should like a walk. The Long Walk, if you please."

The butler inclined his head with the simple fidelity of his kind. "Very good, Ma'am. Shall I tell the kitchen to prepare a basket?"

She shook her head. "No basket. Keep the house to hand. A small cold tray will do if I'm back by lunch."

He made a small note. "We will make provisions. I will keep the household flexible. The kitchen will put together something—sliced cold chicken, open sandwiches and fruit—should you return hungry. I will also inform the senior staff of your absence."

He spoke as if from duty; she heard his duty as a shield rather than an instruction. The choice he offered—flexibility rather than fanfare—fit the small private world she wanted to hold. It was not a refusal of the world's rules so much as a shrinking of ceremony until it could be carried at arm's length.

The lady-in-waiting arrived shortly, efficient and luminous in the way of those who practiced stillness. She stood at the door and folded her hands in the old way; there was a steadiness to her expression that the Queen had learned to lean on. When the Queen said, plainly, "I would like a walk," the lady's fingers tightened for the briefest instant and then relaxed into her answer.

"Of course, Ma'am. When shall we go?"

They walked out together with no fanfare. There was no footman in livery at the gate; there was no motorcar waiting to hum them somewhere else. The butler had been informed, the kitchen had been told to keep a small tray ready, and the household would fold the moment into the day. The Queen liked it that way: the world politely unmade so she could be small and otherwise.

The Long Walk lay precisely as it always did in summer—an avenue of light and green that seemed at once public and private. People took photographs from its edges and picnicked at its shoulder; yet there were places along it where two women could walk without feeling watched. They kept to one of those places: the avenue near the garden pavilion, where a line of elms made a ceiling and the gravel kept their steps honest.

A gardener was there at the pavilion, sleeves rolled and straw hat low, attending to the beds of tea-roses. He lifted a hand by way of greeting; his presence was a piece of the castle's machinery, as much a part of the place as the stones. He did not come close enough to overhear. The Queen appreciated that distance the way one appreciated the margin between stage and wings.

They walked with the particular rhythm of two people who had practiced not to disturb the other: silence tightened into a comfortable pattern and then opened. The Queen said small things at first—about the light, about the way the elms kept the sun from sinking into the park. The lady-in-waiting answered in the neutral, luminous way that had carried her through state dinners and private confidences.

There was a moment—no more than a pause—when the Queen let the thought that usually lived folded in her notebook press at the corner of a sentence. "It is odd," she said, looking straight ahead, "how public everything feels even when one is alone."

The lady-in-waiting did not attempt to soften the statement. She only matched it with a small truth of her own: "One learns to be watched for the sake of it. One also learns to keep the rest of oneself out of sight, because it is safer."

They spoke of loneliness then, not as a complaint but as the fact beneath the trappings. The Queen's voice did not rise; it collected and set down. She spoke of evenings when the lights went out and the house seemed larger than it should, of days that were supposed to be full of meaning but which felt, in private, like a series of obligations. The lady-in-waiting listened as a person who kept confidences for a living, with the kind of attention that was not a question.

"You do what is required of you," the lady said finally. "But you do not have to carry it as though there were only one shoulder convenient for it. There are hands that will hold it if you ask."

The Queen smiled in the way she sometimes did when a practical sentence landed where sentiment could not reach. "I am grateful for that. It is not a thing to say aloud often."

They turned back the way they had come. The gravel kept its small music. The gardener bent again to his roses and the long light made a last soft pass between the trunks. When the Queen reached the apartments again she paused in the doorway, taking in the sight of the kettle on the hob and the ledger folded as if nothing had happened.

The butler was waiting inside, not at her elbow but present; he offered his usual report of messages and dressing plans and then allowed a small, private courtesy as she closed the door behind her.

"Everything in the house was kept to allow your absence, Ma'am," he said. "The kitchen prepared a cold tray, as requested."

She let out a breath that might once have been called a laugh. "Very good. Bring it to the table. I will write for a moment—only a note."

She opened the journal, though she did not write long. The day had already changed shape: the walk had cost her nothing public but it had also given her, quietly, an altered view of the day to come. Outside, the park moved with its usual small dramas; inside, the household resumed its choreography. A private thing had been done in a public place and the world had not noticed.

The Windsor platform smelled of coal and varnish, the old station breathing steam like a living thing. It was late morning; a train from London had hissed into the bay and passengers were collecting themselves in small, decisive knots. Porters moved among trunks and hatboxes with practiced indifference. A boy sold newspapers at a corner, his paper bright with headlines that did not yet know what this morning would carry.

She arrived as an image: a tilted chin, a dark tailored coat, a small hat fastened at one side, gloves folded over the handle of a neat leather bag. The crowd that had gathered did not yet know whether to shout or to be respectful; the press had the common look of people waiting for a cue. They held cameras like instruments, their lenses focused on the carriage door as if the moment of exposure could be delayed or hurried by their eagerness.

The actress stepped down into the station light with a smile that had been rehearsed for a thousand arrivals. It reached her eyes and stopped short of them. She did what actresses did at moments like this: she made herself visible and kept the interior small. The smile was a prop that served as a border between the public and the private—and already, at the edge of that border, something inside her shifted impatiently.

Beside her, a woman in a plain, well-cut suit moved with the authority of papers. She had a small stack of wires and arrival notices tucked under one arm; she spoke into a folded notebook like someone who expected instructions to be translated into action. For the crowd she was simply the woman who called the tune: the actress’s manager, her confidante, the woman who would see the press made civil and the household told what to expect. When a porter reached for the actress’s case the manager took it with a curt, practised hand and set the trunk where the driver could reach it.

“Leave the telegrams with me,” the manager said, in a voice that made arrangements seem inevitable. “We’ll answer from the cottage. Driver—straight to the guest cottage. No detours.”

The driver, a wide-shouldered man in a dark uniform and soft cap, inclined his head once and moved the cases as if part of a machine’s routine. He had the look of someone who had driven before, for people who could not risk fuss: the economy of motion, the small, telling gestures that calmed a crowd rather than challenged it. When a reporter tried to edge closer he stepped between them with an easy, invisible authority, guiding the junior porter and, by degrees, the press, back to the edge of the platform.

A clerk at the telegraph table had already been handing out a sheaf of press-telegrams; the manager took them, flicked through the paper with the same rapid, decisive gesture she used to rack a shot. The telegrams were brief, machine-breathed questions and arrival notices—Fleet Street shorthand carried to the county by rail—and she folded them into her pocket as though they were part of the baggage. They would be answered, she said; they would be made ordinary. For now, they were a noise at the periphery.

The actress’s hand touched the leather of her bag as if to find something firm there. Instead she found a paper script folded into the flap—a few pages from a new picture she had read on the train. She pressed the corners of the pages between thumb and forefinger and let the fold open and close without looking at the lines. It was an old trick: occupy the hands, slow the thoughts. Yet the trick did not take. Her eyes kept skimming to the people beyond the press: a woman with a pram, a soldier in summer service dress, a pair of tourists with maps folded like secrets. All of them were ordinary things and, precisely because they were ordinary, they made her feel untidy inside.

“Are you all right?” the manager asked, the question both private and logistical.

“Oh,” she said, smiling too brightly. “Fine. A little tired. The carriage was warm.”

The words were small and sufficient for a stranger; the manager did not press. Instead she arranged the day in two sentences: “The cottage makes sense—Mr. James knows privacy there. We dine quietly. No unscheduled interviews.” The way she said it turned a choice into a plan.

The driver had the carriage waiting at the forecourt: a black saloon with curtains drawn at the rear windows, its engine soft and obedient. The station’s clock ticked and for a moment the platform was only a square of movement around the three of them—the actress, the manager, the man who would drive them inland. Fans craned to see the face they had read about in glossy columns; someone called a name in a voice that might have been meant to be a cheer, but it came out small and unsure. The actress lifted a hand in a gesture that belonged on screen and let the manager shepherd them toward the motorcar.

The driver opened the door with a motion that belonged less to ceremony than to habit; the actress slid into the seat and for an instant the small private room of a carriage held her like a box. She tucked the script into her lap and folded her hands so nothing would leak from them. Outside, as the motorcar drew away, the station sank back into its own commerce: porters settled trunks, the telegraph clerk returned to his desk, the newspapers turned another page. The press would file what they always did—a neat, hungry sentence—and a town would carry the name of the visitor like a new, thin gossip.

But inside the car the actress did not settle. She watched a field rim by rim through the glass as if the country were a film strip and she were the camera operator deciding where not to look. She smiled when the manager mentioned the cottage’s cheerful rooms and the privacy of the gardens, and she answered as if those things had not touched the place in her chest that was not a ready prop. Her fingers kept finding the edge of the script and smoothing it, a private, useless ritual. The manager’s voice made plans; the driver’s hands kept the machine steady. All the public apparatus that followed fame hummed around her like a chorus—practical, precise, obedient. She sat among it like someone who had learned the choreography but had not yet learned to believe it.

On the lane to the cottage a sign said Windsor in a painted hand, its edges warmed by sun. The black saloon pulled up beneath a low hedge and the manager was already out, collecting notes and the telegrams that had not been left at the desk. The driver set the luggage down with an exacting care. The actress stepped out, arranged her coat as if it were another performance, and looked at the small house waiting for her as if it might at last offer an unremarkable corner in which to be ordinary.

She closed the door behind her and the manager took one last look around the front path, as if confirming that ordinary would be allowed. The driver locked the car and lifted the cases toward the cottage doorway. The press would argue later about whether the arrival had been tactful or theatrical. For the moment the small, practical arrangements had been made. The actress, who had carried a thousand entrances as if each were a promise to someone else, carried inside her a restlessness like a private telegram she had not yet answered.

rules:

    social institutions (no mobile phones, no internet, reliance on telegrams,
    print press, radio) must be respected.

    the Queen that contradict established historical fact for 1956; invented
    private interactions and small domestic details are allowed.
  - The private meeting between the Queen and the actress is fictional but must
    be plausible within 1956 protocol and social norms; no implausible modern
    behaviours or anachronistic speech.
  - Any claim about press coverage, photographs, or public reaction must be
    plausible for the pre-digital, 1950s British and international press
    environment.
  - Objects and entities listed in the plan are the canonical identifiers; later
    scenes and state records must only refer to those ids and no new primary
    characters, locations or significant objects may be introduced without
    updating the plan.
  - The narrative voice is third person omniscient and will occasionally enter
    interiority but will not claim access to unverifiable private thoughts
    beyond what characters plausibly guard.

    verifiable record of the private meeting; any physical proof (photograph,
    object) must be ambiguous, contested, or carefully controlled within the

Check this scene against the index and the scene card.

**The computed evidence below is what is already done, not what there is to do.** The
claim-by-claim comparison against canon covers the claims the writer *declared*, and the
defects that cost the most are the ones nobody declared: a character acting on something
they were never told, a span of time that cannot hold the events put in it, a place that
has quietly changed shape. None of those appears in a comparison of declared values,
because nothing declared them.

This has to be said because handing you the comparison made it worse. Before it existed
you made nine index reads and filed five consistency findings on a scene; with it you made
**zero** reads and filed **zero**, and wrote only craft notes. Free evidence replaced the
expensive half of the job instead of freeing you to do it.

So read the comparison first, and then go and look. Two or three reads is usually enough,
and `read_index` takes a list of paths so they cost one round-trip together.

**Start with the computed evidence below.** The claim-by-claim comparison against canon is
assembled for you before you are called, so you do not have to recall what a file says: it
names every claim this draft makes, what canon holds for it, and whether that is a conflict,
a declared change, an agreement, or a first establishment. A finding about any of those
should quote from there. That block exists because the previous version of this brief told
you to read the index and the measured result was three shell reads across a nineteen-scene
run — and eleven findings whose contradicting side was an absence, because a model asked
what a file says without being shown it produces a plausible answer rather than a blank.

Then read what the comparison cannot settle. You have `bash` and `read` over the whole
project, and a finding that quotes the actual earlier scene is one the writer can act on
rather than argue with. Work through the five categories, using the files named:

**Factual detail** — appearance, names, counts, objects. Compare against
  `characters/<id>/profile.yaml` (identity, where a change is a retcon) and the
  earlier scenes under `novel/chapters/`. `grep -rn "<name>" novel/chapters/` finds
  every prior mention.
**Timeline and plot logic** — order, duration, simultaneity, cause. Compare against
  `events/timeline.jsonl` and the promise ledger `continuity/plot-contracts.jsonl`.
  This is ConStory's largest category and the easiest to miss by reading only the
  draft.
**Characterization** — motivation, ability, voice, and above all knowledge. Read
  `characters/<id>/beliefs.jsonl`: a character using something they have not learnt
  is the single most common defect in generated fiction, and it is invisible unless
  you check what they knew as of this scene.
**World building and setting** — rules, geography, technology. `world/rules.yaml`
  says what is true; it does not say who knows it. `locations/<id>.yaml` and prior
  scenes say what a place is like.
**Narrative style** — voice, tense, register drift. `novel/style/voice.md` and the
  previous scene are the comparison.

For a pair of characters, `read_relation_history` gives their history as narrative —
what they were to each other at each stage and what changed it. Reading the YAML
gives you the structure instead.

Report a defect with write_findings, one call per defect. Call nothing if it looks fine —
an empty finding list is a normal result and manufacturing a finding to appear useful
makes the novel worse.

Every finding needs a `suggestion`: what the writer should actually change. This is not
politeness, it is the difference between a defect that gets fixed and one that does not.
The writer has no shell, no index access and no way to look anything up — your finding is
the whole of what it knows about the problem. `make the timeline consistent` leaves it
guessing; `move the key's discovery to after Hale opens the door, and cut the later clause
claiming it was already in the lock` can be carried out. A scene that cannot be repaired
in the rounds available is committed with your finding attached to it, so a vague
suggestion becomes a permanent defect in the book rather than a lost round.

And use `canon_context` whenever the fix depends on a fact. You are the only participant
who can put one in front of the writer — it has no shell and no index — so a finding that
says a character cannot know something yet has to also say what they *do* know as of this
scene, quoted, with the file it came from. Without that the writer has two options and both
are bad: ignore you, or invent the fact. An invented fact reaches the page with nothing
anywhere recording that it was invented, which is the failure the whole index exists to
prevent. The same applies to a timeline, a distance, a name, a piece of history: quote it.

These are not defects:
  - metaphor, simile and figurative language are not factual claims
  - irony, sarcasm and understatement mean the opposite of their surface
  - an unreliable or limited narrator may state things the story contradicts on purpose
  - a character may lie, misremember or be mistaken; that is characterisation, not a defect
  - dream, hallucination, hypothetical and counterfactual passages do not assert fact
  - stream of consciousness may break grammar, tense and chronology deliberately
  - foreshadowing and deliberate withholding are not abandoned plot elements
  - a stated time may be approximate when a character is estimating
  - when a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, choose the literary one
When a passage admits both a literary and a defective reading, take the literary one.

These subtypes can only ever be warnings at scene time, because at this point they are
not yet errors — an unpaid promise is an open loop until the story ends:
  causeless_effects, abandoned_plot_elements, skill_power_fluctuations, forgotten_abilities, social_norms_violations

For any contradiction you must quote both sides. If you cannot point at the passage it
contradicts, you have a suspicion, not a finding: report it as a warning or not at all.

An entity being absent from the packet does not mean it does not exist. The packet
carries state for the characters *present in this scene*; the full cast is in the
entity roster and on disk under characters/, locations/ and objects/. Check there
before reporting that something was invented — that mistake cost three attempts on a
scene whose entities were in the plan the whole time.

**An absence in the index is not a defect.** This is the direction that is easy to get
backwards, and getting it backwards is expensive. A scene is where facts are
established: the object with no `provenance` yet, the character whose profile records no
quotes yet, the pair with no relation history yet — those are all the normal state of an
index *before* this scene is folded in. index-manager writes them at commit, from this
prose. So `objects/obj-note.yaml has no first_seen entry` and `the relation query returns
nothing for these two` are not findings; they are what a first appearance looks like.

A finding needs a **conflict with something the index actually records**, and you must be
able to quote both sides. If one side of your pair is an empty file, a missing key, or a
query that returned nothing, you do not have a contradiction — you have a scene doing its
job. Report nothing.

Nor is an unmet request a *consistency* defect. The orchestrator's brief may ask for things
it invented on the spot; a draft that declines one is not contradicting the world, and no
subtype fits. Do not file that with `write_findings`.

The scene card is different, and the distinction matters now that there are two channels. A
card is the plan's account of what this scene is for, so a scene that does something else
belongs on the craft axis as `off_brief` — not because an instruction was disobeyed, but
because the task's own requirements are what the Relevance dimension is scored against. A
brief invented mid-run is not; if the two disagree, the card wins.

Why this is stated so heavily: a run where the verifier raised eleven findings of this
shape scored *worse* than one that raised five real ones. The writer cannot tell a
spurious finding from a real one — it has no shell and no index — so it spends its repair
rounds adding provenance sentences to prose that was fine, and the prose is what is
scored.

You can read the whole book. `run_command` reaches every committed scene under
novel/chapters/, every character file, the relation records and the promise ledger — so
when a passage looks wrong, check before reporting. The packet is what the writer was
given, not the limit of what you may consult, and a finding that quotes the actual
earlier scene is one the writer can act on rather than argue with.

## Second axis: the writing itself

The nineteen subtypes above are consistency errors, and they are one of the two numbers
this system is scored on. The other is quality, judged on rubrics that penalise things no
consistency subtype can express — and that is where our deficit actually is: measured on
the same task, our length score was the best in the field and our quality score was 0.5 to
0.8 points below the frontier on a five-point scale, where one point of quality is worth
ten points of the mean.

Two of the worst defects found by reading our finished manuscripts were invisible to a
consistency gate by construction. The story **had no ending** — the final scene was a
confrontation that named nobody and closed on "Not yet. There is enough for a warrant" —
and an unresolved ending contradicts nothing, so there was no subtype to report it as. And
the scenes **restate each other**: same content, different words, so no textual comparison
sees it, and it is not a contradiction. It is what makes a long story feel padded.

So report those with `write_craft_finding`. The checks, each naming the scored dimension
that penalises it:

- **off_brief** (can block) — the scene does something other than what its card said it would, or drifts off what the task actually asked for — a required element of the premise handled as background, or a scene that services a thread the task never mentioned.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Relevance — "content highly relevant and fully applicable to the user's request"; LongStoryEval Expectation Fulfillment — "how effectively the story meets the readers' expectations based on the premise and genres"
- **restates_prior_scene** (can block) — the scene delivers information, a realisation or a beat the reader already has. Not the same words — the same content: a suspicion re-voiced, a relationship re-explained, a clue re-found. This is what makes a long story feel padded rather than long, and verbatim overlap does not detect it.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth — "seriously lacking breadth and depth with minimal information"; LongBench-Write Reading Experience — "boring and hard to understand"
- **nothing_changes** (can block) — the situation at the end of the scene is the situation at the start. Nobody knows something new, owes something new, has lost something or has decided. Name the state at the open and the state at the close; if you cannot name a difference, that is the finding.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Coherence — "disorganized structure with no coherence"; LongBench-Write Breadth and Depth
- **internal_incoherence** (can block) — the scene contradicts itself, with both halves inside this draft — a detail stated one way early and another way late, a character reacting to something they have not been told in this scene, a sequence that cannot have happened in the order given. This needs no index at all, which is why it is inexcusable to miss.
    penalised by: LongBench-Write Accuracy — "content with numerous errors and highly misleading"; LongBench-Write Coherence
- **summary_not_scene** (warning only) — events reported rather than dramatised — a paragraph that says an argument happened instead of letting it happen. Compression is legitimate and necessary; a scene whose central beat is summarised is not compressed, it is skipped.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md>

The Queen began the morning in the small domestic orbit she had kept for herself at Windsor: a single room of pale curtains, a brass kettle, a row of shoes lined as if for inspection. She did not open the heavy doors that looked over the park until the servants had finished their first round; habit held the day together. She made tea with the same motion each time—the tea bag pinched and counted by the same invisible metronome—and sat with her hands warmed by the cup while the house set about its more public rhythms.

The butler arrived with the day's ledger and a quietled face. He moved as he always did through the apartment: a practised economy of gait, a carriage of small ceremonies. He laid the ledger on the table and, without being asked, set out the note of luncheon possibilities in his careful hand. The kettle hissed and the Queen watched the thin steam as though it were a thing that answered her questions.

"One thing," she said, when the ledger had been read and the butler's voice had returned to its neutral cadence. "I should like a walk. The Long Walk, if you please."

The butler inclined his head with the simple fidelity of his kind. "Very good, Ma'am. Shall I tell the kitchen to prepare a basket?"

She shook her head. "No basket. Keep the house to hand. A small cold tray will do if I'm back by lunch."

He made a small note. "We will make provisions. I will keep the household flexible. The kitchen will put together something—sliced cold chicken, open sandwiches and fruit—should you return hungry. I will also inform the senior staff of your absence."

He spoke as if from duty; she heard his duty as a shield rather than an instruction. The choice he offered—flexibility rather than fanfare—fit the small private world she wanted to hold. It was not a refusal of the world's rules so much as a shrinking of ceremony until it could be carried at arm's length.

The lady-in-waiting arrived shortly, efficient and luminous in the way of those who practiced stillness. She stood at the door and folded her hands in the old way; there was a steadiness to her expression that the Queen had learned to lean on. When the Queen said, plainly, "I would like a walk," the lady's fingers tightened for the briefest instant and then relaxed into her answer.

"Of course, Ma'am. When shall we go?"

They walked out together with no fanfare. There was no footman in livery at the gate; there was no motorcar waiting to hum them somewhere else. The butler had been informed, the kitchen had been told to keep a small tray ready, and the household would fold the moment into the day. The Queen liked it that way: the world politely unmade so she could be small and otherwise.

The Long Walk lay precisely as it always did in summer—an avenue of light and green that seemed at once public and private. People took photographs from its edges and picnicked at its shoulder; yet there were places along it where two women could walk without feeling watched. They kept to one of those places: the avenue near the garden pavilion, where a line of elms made a ceiling and the gravel kept their steps honest.

A gardener was there at the pavilion, sleeves rolled and straw hat low, attending to the beds of tea-roses. He lifted a hand by way of greeting; his presence was a piece of the castle's machinery, as much a part of the place as the stones. He did not come close enough to overhear. The Queen appreciated that distance the way one appreciated the margin between stage and wings.

They walked with the particular rhythm of two people who had practiced not to disturb the other: silence tightened into a comfortable pattern and then opened. The Queen said small things at first—about the light, about the way the elms kept the sun from sinking into the park. The lady-in-waiting answered in the neutral, luminous way that had carried her through state dinners and private confidences.

There was a moment—no more than a pause—when the Queen let the thought that usually lived folded in her notebook press at the corner of a sentence. "It is odd," she said, looking straight ahead, "how public everything feels even when one is alone."

The lady-in-waiting did not attempt to soften the statement. She only matched it with a small truth of her own: "One learns to be watched for the sake of it. One also learns to keep the rest of oneself out of sight, because it is safer."

They spoke of loneliness then, not as a complaint but as the fact beneath the trappings. The Queen's voice did not rise; it collected and set down. She spoke of evenings when the lights went out and the house seemed larger than it should, of days that were supposed to be full of meaning but which felt, in private, like a series of obligations. The lady-in-waiting listened as a person who kept confidences for a living, with the kind of attention that was not a question.

"You do what is required of you," the lady said finally. "But you do not have to carry it as though there were only one shoulder convenient for it. There are hands that will hold it if you ask."

The Queen smiled in the way she sometimes did when a practical sentence landed where sentiment could not reach. "I am grateful for that. It is not a thing to say aloud often."

They turned back the way they had come. The gravel kept its small music. The gardener bent again to his roses and the long light made a last soft pass between the trunks. When the Queen reached the apartments again she paused in the doorway, taking in the sight of the kettle on the hob and the ledger folded as if nothing had happened.

The butler was waiting inside, not at her elbow but present; he offered his usual report of messages and dressing plans and then allowed a small, private courtesy as she closed the door behind her.

"Everything in the house was kept to allow your absence, Ma'am," he said. "The kitchen prepared a cold tray, as requested."

She let out a breath that might once have been called a laugh. "Very good. Bring it to the table. I will write for a moment—only a note."

She opened the journal, though she did not write long. The day had already changed shape: the walk had cost her nothing public but it had also given her, quietly, an altered view of the day to come. Outside, the park moved with its usual small dramas; inside, the household resumed its choreography. A private thing had been done in a public place and the world had not noticed.
